1.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two World Bank Microdata data-dictionary pages (sect11h_plantingw2 marketing module; secta3_harvestw2 harvest/sales module) for any published statistic — they list variable labels only, including the buyer/outlet network-code questions that would underpin a channel-of-sale share, but carry no estimates. 2) Checked the GHS-Panel Wave 2 study description page (microdata.worldbank.org/catalog/1952) — scope, sampling and topic list only. 3) Checked the NBS microdata catalog entry (microdata.nigerianstat.gov.ng/catalog/50) — stub record, no tables. 4) Read the NBS 'Select Tables from the GHS Panel Wave 2 2012/13' PDF text (nigerianstat.gov.ng/download/195); its table of tables runs to 23 tables covering demography, ICT access, consumption, expenditure, food availability, shocks, income, plot input use and livestock — no marketing or buyer-outlet table, so the frequently cited 2012/13 'channel of sale' share is not present in the supplied text. 5) Read the post-planting agriculture questionnaire PDF on unstats.un.org — confirms Section 11H 'MARKETING OF AGRICULTURAL SURPLUS' exists, instrument only. 6) Opened the IFPRI NSSP WP 66 PDF text on CGSpace (T2) — only cover, contents and table titles were returned; no numeric result quotable. 7) Opened the IDEAS/RePEc page for the same paper — its abstract does carry quantified findings (thirds of households by sales share) but the domain is tiered T5, from which statistics are inadmissible, and in any case the construct is commercialisation, not formal-market access. 8) Checked the Springer EJDR four-country commercialisation article — Nigeria appears only as one of four APRA study contexts, sub-national and about commercialisation 'capacity', not national formal-market access. 9) Checked the AGRA/KIT PIATA 2019 Nigeria outcome monitoring report (T4) — it has a 'Sales channels (indicator 33)' section for maize in Kaduna and rice in Niger/Kaduna, but the supplied text stops at the contents pages, so no figure could be quoted, and it would in any case be two-state programme-beneficiary data rather than a national smallholder rate. Dead ends throughout; no admissible national figure for the named construct.
1.6.note: Next level not proposed: Even level 1 is withheld because the evidence does not establish any value on the indicator's own scale: nothing in these pages reports what share of Nigerian smallholders sell to, or can reach, formal market channels. To reach level 1 defensibly one would still need a published sub-20% formal-market figure; what exists instead is a share-of-harvest-sold distribution, which cannot be mapped onto formal-channel access without an unpublished assumption. Closest available evidence, recorded as context only and not as the cell value: the IFPRI NSSP working paper 'The relative commercial orientation of smallholder farmers in Nigeria' (Benson, Amare & Ogunniyi 2020), using nationally representative GHS-Panel 2015/16 data, reports on its RePEc/IDEAS abstract page (T5 domain) that about one-third of smallholder farming households made no crop sales at all and another third sold less than one-third of harvested crops by value. That is a COMMERCIALISATION / share-of-output-sold measure, not ACCESS TO FORMAL MARKETS: it does not distinguish formal channels (contract buyers, processors, aggregators, cooperatives, organised/regulated markets) from sales to informal itinerant traders or neighbours, which is precisely what the indicator name asserts. Likewise the GHS-Panel 2012/13 instrument records the largest buyer/outlet by network code, which would yield a channel-of-sale SHARE if tabulated — again participation in a channel, not access. The indicator census question flagged for this row is therefore live here: the only Nigerian evidence in these pages sits on the 'channel of sale / participation' side, not the 'access' side, and no published national percentage of smallholders with access to formal markets was found.
1.6.defnote: The name asserts national smallholder ACCESS to formal markets; Egypt records a regional contract-farming PARTICIPATION rate from seven governorates and Nigeria a 2012/13 channel-of-sale share — two different constructs, neither of which is access, and neither national in Egypt's case.
1.6.name: Smallholder access to formal markets (%)

1.7.value: DATA GAP — Order of examination: (1) IFPRI NSSP Brief 25 'Review of small farmer access to agricultural credit in Nigeria' (CGSpace, T2) — title matches the construct exactly, but only the abstract text was retrieved; its sole quantitative statement is 18 percent of farm households with access to financial services, citing Akramov 2009 on 2006 CWIQ; the brief PDF body was not in the supplied pages. (2) World Bank 'Rural Finance in Nigeria: Integrating New Approaches' (openknowledge, T2) — abstract gives fewer than 2 percent of rural households with institutional finance; wrong unit and wrong scope. (3) CGAP/World Bank 'National Survey and Segmentation of Smallholder Households in Nigeria' (both the documents1.worldbank.org T1 mirror and cgap.org T4 pages) — the retrieved text covers only the introduction/table of contents and the summary page; the financial-inclusion chapter (Section 5) that would contain any borrowing figures is not in the supplied text, and the summary sentence available reports account-based financial inclusion (a quarter), not credit. (4) NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5 2023/24 report (T1) — only front matter and table of contents retrieved; no credit chapter figures present. (5) NBS and World Bank microdata catalog pages — confirm Credit modules exist in GHS-Panel W5 and in the 2016 CGAP survey, but publish no tabulated statistic. (6) RVO/Agri-Logic 'Addressing the $200 billion demand for finance for Agriculture and Agribusiness in Nigeria' (T5) — retrieved text is contents plus a macro indicator table (e.g., domestic credit to private sector 12% of GDP); no farmer credit-access share, and T5 could not carry a statistic in any case. Dead ends: no Findex, CBN Agricultural Credit Guarantee Scheme, or EFInA A2F page was among the supplied sources.
1.7.note: Next level not proposed: No level was proposed because no supplied source states an agricultural-credit access rate for Nigerian farmers; the 18 percent figure that would imply level 2 measures access to financial services generally, and the sub-2 percent figure that would imply level 1 measures rural households rather than farmers and predates 2008. Indicator name asserts share of FARMERS with agricultural CREDIT ACCESS. Nearest available evidence in the supplied pages: IFPRI (CGSpace, T2, 2010) states 'only 18 percent of farm households (mainly smallscale farmers) have access to financial services (Akramov 2009)' — right population (farm households) but wrong service scope (all financial services, not agricultural credit), and the reference year is 2006. World Bank 'Rural Finance in Nigeria' (openknowledge, T2, 2008) states 'fewer than 2 percent of rural households have access to any sort of institutional finance' — wrong population (all rural households, including non-farmers) and wrong service scope (any institutional finance). CGAP's national smallholder survey (T4 on cgap.org, T1 mirror on documents1.worldbank.org) reports that 'Only a quarter of smallholders are financially included, meaning they hold an account registered in their own name at a full-service financial institution' — this is account ownership, not credit, and is a smallholder-household unit rather than a farmer unit. All three are 'access/inclusion' or 'use' measures of finance broadly; none is a credit-access rate for farmers.
1.7.defnote: The name asserts a share of FARMERS with credit ACCESS; Egypt records rural adults aged 15+ (a population that includes non-farmers) and Nigeria records smallholder households, and both measure borrowing/use rather than access.
1.7.name: Agricultural credit access (% farmers)

1.8.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the two NBS T1 microdata pages for a published CSA adoption statistic: catalog/82 study description lists 'Expectations on Climate Extremes and Past Experience' as a community topic and 'Extension Services / Digital Farming Information / Input Use on Plot' in agriculture, but is metadata only. 2) Opened the sectc6b_harvestw5 data dictionary — it lists question c6bq5 items (soil conservation practices, rainwater harvesting, tree planting, improved/heat/drought-tolerant seeds, irrigation intensification) but is a variable list with 2,032 community cases and no tabulated percentages. 3) Opened secta11c2_harvestw5 (plot input use) — herbicide, pesticide, inorganic/organic fertiliser and traction variables, again no percentages. 4) Scanned the GHS-Panel Wave 5 survey report page text: only front matter and table of contents were returned; no climate-smart adoption figure appears in the supplied text. 5) Checked NASC 2022 launch release and NASS 2023 catalog entry — both describe input/technology adoption as an intended output but publish no CSA figure in the supplied text. 6) World Bank 'Toward Climate-Resilient Development in Nigeria' (2013) — supplied text is front matter/contents only, with a chapter on adaptation options and 'The Climate-Smart Way'; no adoption percentage in the retrieved text. 7) IFPRI discussion paper landing page — reports experimental treatment effects (USG adoption up 24 percentage points, +8 with discounts), which is a trial effect size, not a population adoption rate. 8) Springer/CABI article — the only quotable farmer-share figure (87.2%), but zone-limited and trait-based. 9) Agricultura Tropica et Subtropica PDF — 82% adopters, n=377, north-western Nigeria, on a domain tiered T5 here. Dead ends: no FAOSTAT/WDI/ITU-style T1 database series for this construct was among the retrieved pages, and no Nigerian government policy artifact reporting a national CSA adoption rate was surfaced.
1.8.note: sub-national purposive survey samples; not nationally representative; adoption definitions differ between studies. Next level not proposed: No level, including level 1, is proposed because the pages contain no nationally scoped measurement of climate-smart practice adoption by Nigerian farmers at all — the NBS GHS-Panel and NASS pages establish that the underlying questions are asked (climate-response actions in the community module; plot input use) but publish no derived adoption share, and the two studies that do publish shares are zone- and state-limited. Level 5 specifically is not proposed because neither 87.2% nor 82% is a national estimate, and the 87.2% figure counts a climate-resilient crop trait rather than the practices the indicator names. The indicator names the share of FARMERS (country-wide) using climate-smart PRACTICES. The best available evidence differs on two axes. (1) Object: the Springer/CABI study measures farmers who 'adopted at least one climate resilient trait in crops' — a crop-genetics trait, not a practice basket such as conservation tillage, agroforestry, residue management or water harvesting. (2) Geography: it covers smallholders in four states across the North Central and Northwest zones only, not Nigeria as a whole. The second quantified source (Agricultura Tropica et Subtropica, on a domain tiered T5 here) reports that '82 % of the respondents are adopters of the CSA practices' among 377 households in some rural areas of north-western Nigeria — closer to the named construct in object, but an even narrower, non-representative geographic base. The NBS GHS-Panel Wave 5 community questionnaire (section C6B) collects community-level responses on actions taken to reduce climate-event damage (soil conservation, rainwater harvesting, tree planting, improved/heat- and drought-tolerant seeds, irrigation), and the plot-level input module records fertiliser/organic-fertiliser use, but no published tabulation of a farmer-level climate-smart-practice adoption rate appears in the retrieved pages. NASS 2023 and the 2022 NASC list 'use of agricultural inputs and technologies' as a topic but publish no CSA adoption share in the pages supplied.
1.8.defnote: The name counts FARMERS adopting climate-smart practices; Egypt records a share of WHEAT AREA under a single practice and Nigeria a share of farmers in two zones adopting at least one climate-resilient crop TRAIT — land, practice-basket and geographic scope all differ from the name.
1.8.name: Farmers using climate-smart practices (%)

8.1.value: DATA GAP — Checked Source 1 (SOFI 2024 Section 2.1 key messages) — global 9.1% 2023, Africa 20.4%, Asia 8.1%, LAC 6.2%, Oceania 7.3%; no country breakdown. Checked Source 2 (FAO SOFI flagship landing page) — navigational/promotional only, no country data. Checked Source 3 (SOFI 2024 Annex 1A) — this is the correct location for Nigeria's PoU in Table A1.1, but the retrieved text contains only the table heading and footnotes (n.a./n.r. conventions, <2.5 convention, three-year-average rule), not the data rows; Nigeria does not appear in the retrieved text. Checked Sources 4 and 5 (peer-reviewed Nigerian child malnutrition studies) — stunting, wasting, underweight, anaemia, vitamin A deficiency, CIAF; none is PoU. Checked Source 6 (IFRC emergency appeal via ReliefWeb) — IPC acute malnutrition caseloads for North-East/North-West; a different construct and sub-national. Dead ends: FAOSTAT Suite of Food Security Indicators and the SOFI Annex data rows were not among the supplied pages, so the figure could not be retrieved or quote-verified.
8.1.note: Next level not proposed: No level, including level 1, is supported: the evidence does not show any Nigeria-specific PoU value at all, so it cannot even be established that Nigeria's PoU falls below or above the 25 percent cut. The only PoU figures present in the supplied pages are supranational: SOFI 2024 reports global PoU of 9.1 percent in 2023 and Africa at 20.4 percent in 2023. A regional African aggregate is not a Nigeria figure and must not be substituted for one — Nigeria's PoU has historically diverged materially from the continental mean, and the direction of that divergence cannot be inferred from the aggregate. Sources 4-6 report child undernutrition indicators (stunting 7.2-61%, wasting 1-29%, underweight 5.9-42.6%; 5.44m acutely malnourished children in the North-East and North-West), which measure child anthropometric status, not the population-wide prevalence of insufficient dietary energy intake that PoU (SDG 2.1.1) measures. An independent T1 series (World Bank WDI SN.ITK.DEFC.ZS) reports 19.9 for 2023.
8.1.name: Prevalence of undernourishment (%)

8.5.value: FAO's RuLIS country brief for Nigeria (General Household Survey 2018-2019) finds that among owners or rights-bearers of agricultural land in Nigeria, about a third are women, with significantly more men than women holdin
8.5.src: FAO, RuLIS country brief: Nigeria (Nigeria General Household Survey 2018-2019)
8.5.note: Rounded qualitative expression ("about a third") rather than a published point estimate; derived from a household survey (GHS 2018-19) and conflicts with a lower government policy claim reported in the press. Next level not proposed: Level 4 would require published evidence that women make up more than 40 percent of agricultural land owners or rights-bearers in Nigeria. No retrieved source shows this; FAO's phrasing caps the estimate at roughly a third, and the other retrieved figures point lower still (DHS 2018: 4.2% of women aged 15-49 own land alone; Federal Ministry of Women Affairs, as reported in Punch, claims women are a small minority of landowners). No source establishes a share above 40 percent. The quoted FAO figure is SDG 5.a.1(b) — share of women among owners or rights-bearers of AGRICULTURAL land — i.e. it sits on the OWNERSHIP side of the unratified definition question, which matches the indicator's name ("women who own land") rather than the operator/holder alternative; the denominator is owners/rights-bearers of agricultural land, not all agricultural holders, so it is a close but not identical reading of "% holders". Two other figures in the retrieved pages do NOT measure this construct and are recorded here only as context: (a) the World Bank Gender Data Portal (DHS 2018) reports Nigeria 4.2% for "Women who own land alone (% of women age 15-49)" — a different denominator (all women of reproductive age, not landowners/holders) and restricted to sole ownership; (b) Punch (T5 news) reports the Federal Ministry of Women Affairs WEE policy stating "Only one in five landowners in Nigeria is female. This accounts for only 10 per cent of all landowners in Nigeria" — internally inconsistent, T5, and not usable for a statistic.
8.5.tier_detail: Rounded qualitative expression ("about a third") rather than a published point estimate; derived from a household survey (GHS 2018-19) and conflicts with a lower government policy claim reported in the press
8.5.defnote: The indicator name says women who OWN land while the canonical statistic counts women agricultural holders (operators), who may rent rather than own.
8.5.name: Women who own land (% holders)

2.1.value: DATA GAP — 1) ITU Digital Development Dashboard for Nigeria (ddd_NGA.pdf, T1) — found national coverage: 94% mobile-cellular, 87% at-least-3G, 81% at-least-4G (2022); the only rural-tagged row is households with Internet access at home, rural (2017) 2%, a different construct. No rural coverage split. 2) ITU DataHub landing page and UMC dashboard — both rendered with United States as focus economy and no Nigeria values; no rural coverage indicator value retrievable. 3) ITU Statistics page — confirms ITU publishes 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area' but only as global/regional/development-group aggregates, not as a Nigeria country figure; dead end for a national-country rural cell. 4) ITU DataHub About page — methodology only, confirms mobile population coverage is collected as total, 3G, and 4G-and-above, with no rural split in the country questionnaire; this explains why no Nigeria rural figure exists at T1. 5) NCC Network Performance Report index (T3) — lists an 'Urban Vs Rural Analysis' section in the Q2 2026 report, the most promising route to a rural figure, but the retrieved text is navigation only, no percentage. 6) NCC 'The Technology Driving Your Connection' (T3) — qualitative rural statements about 3G prevalence and underserved-region throughput deficits of 40-50%, but throughput, not coverage. 7) GSMA SSA 2024 Year in Review (T4) — Africa-wide coverage gap of 11% (2023), not Nigeria and not rural; inadmissible for a prerequisite row regardless. 8) GSMA Coverage Maps page (T4) — tool description only, no Nigeria value. 9) nPerf Nigeria coverage map (T5) — crowdsourced map with no published percentage; T5 barred from carrying a statistic. Conclusion: no admissible, quotable rural figure in the supplied pages.
2.1.note: Closest available T1 evidence is national-level, not rural; operator-reported administrative coverage estimates. Next level not proposed: Level withheld rather than set below 5 as well: the evidence does not even support a defensible statement-based banding. The qualitative NCC finding that 3G 'remains prevalent in rural and underserved areas' establishes that some rural mobile broadband service exists but gives no share of rural population covered, so it cannot be argued past or below any of the 20/40/60/80 cut points. What is missing and would settle it: the ITU urban/rural disaggregated 'population covered by at least a 3G/4G mobile network' value for Nigeria, or the rural coverage percentage inside an NCC quarterly Network Performance Report. The indicator names RURAL mobile broadband coverage. The best T1 evidence in the supplied pages is national: ITU's Nigeria dashboard reports population covered by at least a 3G mobile network (2022) at 87% and population covered by at least a 4G mobile network (2022) at 81%, plus mobile-cellular network coverage of 94%. These are whole-population figures with no urban/rural split, so they cannot stand in for rural coverage — in Nigeria the coverage gap is concentrated precisely in rural and remote LGAs, so a national figure will overstate the rural value by an unknown margin. The one rural-disaggregated ITU figure visible on that page is a different indicator entirely: households with Internet access at home, rural (2017) 2%. On the unratified definitional question flagged in the indicator census: this row should be judged against RURAL as named, which means the Egypt-style national at-least-3G number is not admissible here; ITU does publish 'Population covered by a mobile-cellular and a mobile-broadband network, total and by urban/rural area' as a global/regional time series (per the ITU Statistics page), but that is an aggregate release, not a Nigeria country value, and no Nigeria rural cell appears in any supplied page.
2.1.defnote: The name asserts RURAL coverage, but Egypt's row records the ITU national at-least-3G figure as a clean cls="Measured" number that scores level 5 mechanically, while Nigeria records a rural-but-4G-only modelled estimate — so the register's only universal connectivity prerequisite carries a…
2.1.name: Rural mobile broadband coverage (3G/4G)

2.4.src: ITU DataHub — Nigeria data (Individuals using the Internet)

The quoted figure is sex-disaggregated (female) account ownership for Nigeria, which is exactly what the indicator names. Two caveats bearing on the unratified definition: (a) the underlying WDI series is FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS, 'Account ownership at a financial institution OR with a mobile-money-service provider, female (% of population ages 15+)', which reports 52.22 for Nigeria 2024 — i.e. mobile-money accounts are counted inside the total, the same construct scored separately at 8.4, so mobile money is double-weighted in the FIN column as the census note flags; (b) the corresponding all-adult figure is not the answer to this cell — for context the male figure is 74.3% and the Gender Data Portal notes a 22.1 point male-female gap, larger than the Sub-Saharan Africa gap of 12.1. Corroborated by an independent T1 series (World Bank WDI FX.OWN.TOTL.FE.ZS (Global Findex wave)): 52.22 for 2024.

8.2.name: Account ownership, female (%)

(5) Findex 2021 Chapter 1 headline brief and Executive Summary PDF — give the Sub-Saharan Africa regional figure (33 percent of adults have a mobile money account) and global/developing-economy aggregates, but no Nigeria figure; a regional figure is not a country figure. Dead end: the specific series that would answer this cell (Findex 'Mobile money account (% age 15+)' for Nigeria) was not among the retrieved pages.
8.4.note: Next level not proposed: Withheld rather than scored: no supplied page states a weighted, population-representative percentage of Nigerian adults aged 15+ holding a mobile money account, so even the lowest cut point (10%) cannot be tested against a verified figure. Two near-misses were considered and rejected. (1) World Bank WDI 'Account ownership at a financial institution or with a mobile-money-service provider (% of population ages 15+)' lists Nigeria 2024 = 63.26 — this is a combined bank-or-mobile-money measure, not the mobile money account share, and using it would massively overstate the named construct. 8.6.value: DATA GAP — 1) Checked the three World Bank Findex 2025 Nigeria microdata pages (catalog/7957 variable F1/V145 for con8, and two renderings of the data dictionary) for a sex-disaggregated phone-ownership statistic — found only the variable definition for con8 (household ownership, unweighted case counts carrying an explicit warning against reading them as population statistics) and a bare variable list including 'female' and 'urbanicity'; no tabulated indicator values. 2) Checked the Findex 2025 publication landing page — global/LMIC headline only ('84% of adults in LMICs own a mobile phone'), no country breakdown. 3) Checked the Findex Policy Research Talk PDF — states 'Mobile phone ownership is widespread, though women are less likely than men to own one' as a slide title, a qualitative direction statement with no Nigeria figure. 4) Checked the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025 PDF text — retrieved portion covers cover matter, contents and introduction only; no country table reached. 5) Checked the GSMA gender-gap-2025 landing page — LMIC aggregates (8% ownership, 14% smartphone, 14% mobile internet) only, relative-gap basis, no Nigeria. 6) Checked technext24 (T5) — headline gives 39% of Nigerian women owning a smartphone but the body carries no Nigeria male comparator and news tier cannot carry a statistic. 7) Checked the Taylor & Francis article on gender variation in telecommunication use in rural Akure North LGA, Nigeria — a 495-household local survey on travel behavior; retrieved text is navigation chrome plus abstract, contains no ownership rates by sex and in any case is one LGA, not national. Dead end on all seven; recording a ratification hold.
8.6.note: Next level not proposed: Withheld rather than scored: the pages supplied contain no Nigeria male phone-ownership rate and no Nigeria female phone-ownership rate on the same basis, which is the minimum required to state any percentage-point gap; and no publisher in this set states a Nigeria pp gap directly. Context, not an answer to this cell: the GSMA Mobile Gender Gap Report 2025 landing page states the LMIC-aggregate gender gap in overall mobile ownership was 8% in 2024 and the smartphone gap 14% — these are (i) low- and middle-income-country aggregates across 15 surveyed markets, not Nigeria, and (ii) relative gaps expressed as a percentage of male ownership, which is exactly the basis mismatch the indicator census flags: the indicator name fixes the unit as percentage points, so the GSMA number cannot be transcribed into this cell even if a Nigeria-level version were available in these pages. The one Nigeria-specific gender figure surfaced is in a T5 news headline (technext24: 'Only 39% of Nigerian women own a smartphone'), which is (i) smartphones rather than phones, (ii) a single-sex level with no corresponding male figure from which to compute a gap, and (iii) news tier, which may not carry a statistic. The Findex Nigeria microdata variable con8 asks 'Does anyone in your household currently own a mobile phone?' — household-level ownership, not individual ownership, and therefore not decomposable by respondent sex into a personal-ownership gap.
8.6.defnote: The name fixes the unit as percentage points but not the sign convention or the basis, so a reversed gap (women ahead) scores as best-in-class under direction L, and the widely quoted GSMA figure for the same construct is a relative gap on a male-ownership base, a different number entirely.
8.6.name: Gender gap in phone ownership (pp)

Dead end: no admissible Nigerian figure available for quotation.
8.9.note: Next level not proposed: Level 1 was not proposed because no source in the supplied pages states any percentage of Nigerian smallholders reached by digital services; the GHS-Panel Wave 5 Section 12 microdata that could yield such a percentage is documented but not tabulated in the retrieved text, and the 10% figure that exists belongs to the LMIC aggregate, not to Nigeria. Context, not an answer: the 60 Decibels page (T5) states that in Low- and Middle-Income Countries digital agriculture solutions 'now have around 50 million active users, covering about 10% of smallholder farming households' — this is a cross-LMIC aggregate, not a Nigeria figure, and cannot be carried into a Nigeria cell. The same page reports a Nigeria farmer survey of 1,374 farmers (2023-24 season, 42% female, 22% smartphone access) conducted with NBS and the World Bank LSMS, but the retrieved text carries no Nigerian reach percentage. Separately, the World Bank microdata catalog for GHS-Panel Wave 5 documents 'sect12_plantingw5.dta ... Section 12 (Digital Farming Information) ... records household-level information on the farmers access, use, and experience with digital farming services', i.e. the raw variables from which a national share could be computed exist, but no published figure appears. On the unratified definitional question: the underlying Nigerian instrument measures farm households that sought/received information or advice via digital channels — a 'reached/used' concept over farming households generally, not a smallholder-delimited (e.g. <2 ha) universe, so even the best available Nigerian evidence sits on the wrong side of the indicator's SMALLHOLDER wording as well as lacking a published headline number.

8.9.name: Smallholders reached by digital services (%)

8.11.note: Next level not proposed: No level above 0 was proposed because no admissible (T1-T4) source in the supplied pages states any figure, band, or bounded qualitative finding for the share of Nigerian agricultural or public digital services offered in local languages; the NITDA standard shows a localisation requirement exists on paper but gives no measurement of how many services meet it. Nearest available evidence sits on the wrong side of the open definitional question in two ways. (1) Domain: the EFInA piece (https://efina.org.ng/2026/04/15/local-language-interfaces-a-critical-innovation-gap-in-nigerian-fintech/, T5) concerns digital FINANCIAL services, not agricultural advisory/extension or e-government services, and characterises them qualitatively as operating almost exclusively in English; it also cites education-related exclusion figures (A2F 2023) that measure financial exclusion, not language coverage of services. (2) Form: it publishes no numerator/denominator for share of services offered in local languages, which is precisely the gap the indicator census flags. 8.11.name: Services in local languages (%)

8.12.value: A randomized controlled trial of the RiceAdvice digital personalized-extension app in Nigeria found that farm households receiving personalized advice increased their yield by 7% and their profit by 10%.
8.12.src: American Journal of Agricultural Economics (Wiley) — Arouna, Michler, Yergo & Saito, 'One Size Fits All? Experimental Evidence on the Digital Delivery of Personalized Extension Advice in Nigeria'
8.12.note: Experimental estimate from a single-country RCT with a defined study area; not a national-level impact figure. Next level not proposed: Level 5 was not proposed because scale_evidence is empty: none of the supplied pages publish reach figures for the digital services whose impact is documented — no user, subscriber, coverage or geographic-spread numbers for RiceAdvice or comparable Nigerian digital advisory platforms appear in the retrieved text. The trial sample size and study-area extent are not stated in the fetched page, and the only large reach figure available (61,171 beneficiaries, World Bank APPEALS ISR) belongs to a non-digital agro-processing project and cannot be borrowed for this row. Impact evidence therefore remains at the level of localized experiments rather than a documented, nationally scaled impact record. The evidence sits on the correct side of the census's open question: the measured outcomes are yield (+7%) and profit (+10%) from a digital advisory tool (RiceAdvice mobile app) in Nigeria, i.e. yield/income outcomes rather than diffusion or adoption of digital tools. A second Nigerian digital-extension RCT (Oyinbo et al., 'Digital extension, price risk, and farm performance', AJAE 2022) reports that site-specific digital recommendations 'improve fertilizer management practices and maize yields' with 'only incremental increases in investments and net revenues', but the page supplied for it is an IDEAS/RePEc bibliographic listing (T5), so it is recorded here only as corroborating context, not as the quoted source. Other supplied Nigerian impact studies (innovation platforms on maize income, PMC10208796; improved soybean varieties on yield and revenue, PMC9539571) measure non-digital interventions and therefore do not evidence digital-agriculture impact. World Bank APPEALS ISR figures (62.62% productivity increase, 61,171 beneficiaries) are for a general agro-processing project, not a digital service.
8.12.tier_detail: Experimental estimate from a single-country RCT with a defined study area; not a national-level impact figure
8.12.defnote: The name's parenthetical fixes the outcome as yield or income, but Egypt's level 3 rests on an evaluation whose measured outcome is diffusion and adoption of digital tools, not yield or income.
8.12.name: Documented impact evidence (yield/income)
